samples.text:
The graph shows how much electricity was produced from coal, natural gas and renewables in one country from 1990 until 2025.

Firstly, coal was the biggest source at the beginning. It was 210 terawatt hours in 1990 and it increase to 232 in 2000. After that it decreased a lot, and it was 130 in 2015 and 70 in 2020. In 2025 coal was only 35 terawatt hours, which is the lowest of the three source.

Secondly, natural gas started at only 20 terawatt hours in 1990. It grew quickly and reached a peak of 140 in 2010. Then it went down slowly to 120 in 2020 and 105 in 2025. In 2015 gas was more than coal for the first time.

Also, renewables was very low in the beginning, only 8 terawatt hours. It stayed low until 2005 but then it rise rapidly. In 2020 it was 140 and in 2025 it reached 190, the highest of all.

In conclusion, coal fell a lot and renewables rose a lot, while natural gas went up and then down.
samples.why: Overview given only in the final line · main trends covered but mechanically sequenced (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · repetitive vocabulary · agreement and tense errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The line graph illustrates the quantity of electricity produced from three sources, namely coal, natural gas and renewables, in a particular country over the period 1990 to 2025.

It is clear that the country's energy mix changed dramatically. Coal went from being the dominant source to the least important one, while renewables rose from a negligible level to become the main source by the end of the period. Natural gas rose and then declined moderately.

Coal generated 210 TWh in 1990 and peaked at 232 TWh in 2000. From then on, its output fell continuously, dropping to 130 TWh in 2015 and to just 35 TWh by 2025. Natural gas, on the other hand, expanded rapidly from 20 TWh to a high of 140 TWh in 2010, and it overtook coal in 2015. After that, however, it decreased gradually to 105 TWh.

Renewables provided only 8 TWh in 1990 and grew slowly for the first fifteen years. From 2005 onwards, generation from this source accelerated sharply, surpassing both of the other fuels by 2020, when it reached 140 TWh, and finally climbing at 190 TWh in 2025.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying the reversal of coal and renewables · logical progression · good range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary · mostly accurate grammar with one preposition slip.

samples.text:
The graph compares electricity output from coal, natural gas and renewable sources in one country across a 35-year period from 1990 to 2025.

Overall, the data reveal a fundamental shift in the country's energy supply. Coal, initially by far the largest source, declined steeply after 2000, whereas renewables, which were almost insignificant in 1990, became the leading source by 2020. Natural gas occupied a middle position, rising to a peak before tapering off.

In 1990, coal accounted for 210 TWh, dwarfing the output of natural gas (20 TWh) and renewables (8 TWh). Coal-fired generation edged up to a high of 232 TWh in 2000 but then went into sustained decline, falling to 130 TWh in 2015 and to a mere 35 TWh by 2025, around one sixth of its 1990 level.

Natural gas, meanwhile, expanded seven-fold to 140 TWh in 2010 and briefly overtook coal in 2015, before slipping back to 105 TWh. The most spectacular growth, however, was in renewables. After modest gains to 25 TWh in 2005, output surged, outstripping both gas and coal by 2020 at 140 TWh and reaching 190 TWh in 2025.
samples.why: Skilful selection of key features · well-placed overview capturing the shift in energy mix · accurate figures and derived comparisons · wide, precise vocabulary · varied, error-free sentence structures.
